title: An exploratory evaluation of perceptual, psychoacoustic and acoustical properties of urban soundscapes
research_question: To explore the multi-dimensional space involved in listening to soundscape recordings made in different city-based settings, examining perceptual, psychoacoustic, and acoustical properties using statistical methods.

participants.description: Fifteen native English-speaking normal-hearing participants (aged 21-55) for the level-matched soundscape clips. Five participants (aged 21-40) for the initial 219 clips.
participants.recruitment: Not explicitly stated, but implies recruitment for listening tasks.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: 219 urban soundscape clips, 8s duration, 50ms onset/offset ramps, 18dB overall SPL range. Later, a subset of 150 clips, level-matched to 71dB (A-weighted scale), with dominant sound sources equally distributed across natural (N=50), human (N=52), and mechanical (N=48) categories.

findings.mechanism: Principal components analysis identified underlying dimensions of emotional response.
findings.quote: The first component explained 48% of the variance and had high positive loadings for the semantic scales of pleasantness, calmness, comfort and intrusiveness.

findings.mechanism: Principal components analysis identified underlying dimensions of emotional response.
findings.quote: The second component explained 24% of the variance and had high positive loadings for the two other semantic scales (vibrancy and informational content).

findings.mechanism: Curve estimation regression indicated a weak quadratic relationship, but the V-shape was not clearly apparent.
findings.quote: Curve estimation regression statistics using a model with linear and quadratic terms indicated some degree of significant relationship (p < 0.01) However, the amount of variance explained by the models did not exceed 6%.

findings.mechanism: Equating sound level did not reveal a systematic relationship between pleasantness and vibrancy, suggesting they are independent dimensions for urban soundscapes.
findings.quote: Again, curve estimation regression statistics were computed using a model with linear and quadratic terms. There was no evidence for a relationship between the two semantic scales (p > 0.05).

findings.mechanism: Different sound sources evoke different emotional responses, influenced by interpretation and context.

mechanisms: The emotional experience of real environments (soundscapes) is too complex to be captured by two motivational factors (pleasantness and arousal) alone, as clips often contain numerous sound sources within a rich contextual situation.
The overall emotional experience, especially arousal intensity, is modulated by the interpretation of the sound source properties within their social and geographical context.
The perceived quality of a soundscape is a very individual subjective experience, likely embedded within contextual domains, personal preference, past history, and other social and cultural factors.
The auditory brain transforms input signals at subcortical and cortical stages, meaning sounds are not coded as faithful representations of the input signal.
moderators: Sound level (controlled in a subset of stimuli)
Dominant sound source category (natural, human, mechanical)
Individual differences (implied by low inter-subject agreement)
implementation_implications: Sound level measures alone are insufficient for assessing acoustic comfort in urban planning; richer evaluations of soundscape quality are needed.

Urban planners should consider the multi-factorial nature of soundscape experience, including dominant sound sources, listener interpretation, and context, rather than relying solely on quantitative acoustic analysis.

tables.description: Details of the semantic scales that were used for rating the perceptual attributes of the urban soundscape clips.
The six principal components computed from ratings of 219 urban soundscape clips.

The final stage of the principal components analysis recomputes the component loadings, after excluding those components that explain little of the overall variance. The results for the present study are reported in the first two columns and differ little from the values reported in Table 2. For comparison, results reported by Guillen and Lopéz Barrio [10] are presented alongside. Despite methodological differences (e.g. stimuli, semantic anchors and number of semantic scales), the outputs are remarkably similar.
Details of the best-fitting models that describe the acoustical and psychoacoustic predictors of soundscape pleasantness and vibrancy.

limitations: The study's findings are based on laboratory-based evaluations of soundscape clips, which may not fully capture the complexity of real-world experiences.
The low inter-subject agreement (Kappa values) for pleasantness and vibrancy ratings suggests high individual variability, making it difficult to generalize findings based on group averages.

The low explanatory power of acoustic and psychoacoustic models for pleasantness and vibrancy indicates that significant non-acoustic factors (e.g., context, personal preference, social/cultural factors) are not fully captured.
The study did not explicitly instruct listeners to introspect about context factors governing their judgments of quality, which could be a source of variance.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Subjective perception of soundscapes can be systematically measured and related to objective acoustical and psychoacoustic parameters, contributing to a holistic soundscape evaluation framework.
Human perception of sound is influenced by specific psychoacoustic parameters (e.g., loudness, sharpness, roughness) which can be derived from physical sound properties.

mechanism_chain.description: The paper investigates how objective acoustical properties of urban soundscapes are processed through psychoacoustic mechanisms, leading to subjective perceptual attributes, which in turn form higher-level emotional and evaluative responses.
